source.title: ECO: Quantized Training without Full-Precision Master Weights
source.authors: Mahdi Nikdan; A. Zandieh; Dan Alistarh; V. Mirrokni

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports held-out validation losses across a model-size sweep, but does not fit or test the original scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: Section 4.2 reports final validation losses for six model sizes. Training tokens increase with parameter count (100 N tokens), so the sweep does not isolate parameters from tokens. The paper does not fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal allocations. Other reported fine-tuning and benchmark results compare quantization methods rather than testing scaling-law predictability.
record.test_reason: The study uses a Chinchilla-based token allocation to evaluate quantized-training methods. Section 4.2 compares validation losses at six sizes, jointly increasing parameters and tokens from 30M/3B to 800M/80B. It does not assess power-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or fitted-law sensitivity. Declining loss alone does not test V1, and optimizer failures do not establish a scaling-law failure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that ECO removes master weights without additional persistent memory, avoids naive-removal instability, and nearly matches master-weight baselines while improving the memory–loss trade-off. They qualify this by noting stronger performance with stochastic rounding and a higher noise floor with round-to-nearest. They do not validate scaling-law equations.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests a quantized-training optimizer against master-weight and other quantization baselines; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling-study losses vary by accumulation method and rounding choice; the authors report that ECO gains are smaller with round-to-nearest than with stochastic rounding.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 30M–800M models, ECO with stochastic rounding nearly recovers master-weight validation losses; naive round-to-nearest removal diverges at every size. At 800M, BF16 loss is 2.5306, ECO with stochastic rounding is 2.5399, and naive stochastic rounding is 2.9471.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Error compensation enables low-precision training without master weights while substantially preserving validation loss, especially with stochastic rounding.

record.problems: For the scaling-law claim, the sweep changes token count in proportion to parameter count, does not report compute, and does not fit or assess power-law curves. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the table values.

untested.parts: Power-law form over several orders of magnitude under non-bottleneck conditions; the sweep jointly varies parameters and tokens without assessing that form.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted to small runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute and their scaling exponents; the Chinchilla allocation is used as a reference.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes; fine-tuning compares methods at one model size.
Downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss; benchmarks compare quantization methods.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the extracted V1 limits_scope verdict: failure to test power-law form is an untested component, not evidence limiting its scope. Differences in optimizer accuracy do not by themselves test V7.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss across model sizes while tokens scale jointly with parameter count; does not fit a power law or independently test parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
The fine-tuning experiment does not test power-law form across training regimes or modalities.
Benchmark results compare quantization methods; they do not test downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, fitting choices, or compute-optimal splits are compared.
